newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - U.S. analysts upbeat on Asia.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - U.S. analysts upbeat on Asia.

text.p: The "Year of the Rat" has turned out to be not so fat for Asian economies.
For the first time in a decade, a slowdown in exports raised doubts that the Asian tigers might be losing their economic prowess.

Compared with the first half of 1995, exports fell in China, and the growth rate notably flattened in four tiger economies -- Singapore, Hong Kong, Taiwan and South Korea -- as well as in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

At the same time, Latin American countries are pulling out of recession to post impressive year-on-year growth. Mexico stunned the market with a 7.2-percent rise in Gross Domestic Product (GDP) for the second quarter.
So, has the wheel of fortune turned?

Pessimism about Asia is premature, U.S. economists and money managers say. Even with growth rates moderating, Asia still stands head and shoulders above other world regions. Given a history of boom-and-bust cycles in the Latin American economies, the current recovery could be ephemeral, they say.
As long as Asians continue to squirrel away a hefty chunk of their income, U.S. investors will keep Asia ahead of other emerging markets in their long-term strategies.
ASIA TEXTBOOK CASE OF SAVINGS AND INVESTMENTS

Asia provides a textbook case of savings and investments, argues John Praveen, international economist at Merrill Lynch. "Higher savings lead to higher domestic investments; that, in turn, boosts GDP growth and attracts foreign invesntments."

Asian countries with an average savings rate above 30 percent are the biggest savers in the world. Between 1990 and 1995, Singapore residents saved around 48 percent, Koreans 36 percent, Chinese 39 percent and residents of Hong Kong 35 percent, he said.
According to International Monetary Fund (IMF) data, Asia is the only region in the emerging markets whose savings and investment rates as a percentage of GDP continued rising, Praveen said.
Because of the sound economic fundamentals, Asia received half of the $207.4 billion in capital flows to the emerging markets in 1994. Latin America got a quarter, Praveen said.
With the trends of high savings and investments in place, Asia will lead the world in economic growth into the next century, he said.
For the next decade (1995-2005), the World Bank projects a 7.9-percent annual growth rate for East Asian countries, 5.4 percent for South Asian countries and 3.8 percent for Latin America.
HIGH LEVEL OF SAVINGS CUSHIONS UNCERTAINTY

Ismail Dalla, president of Washington Asset Management, Inc, said the high level of savings and domestic investments provides a cushion for the impact of a cyclical slowdown, political uncertainty and currency swings.
The current export slowdown was brought on in part by the global glut of electronic goods and a collapse of semi-conductor prices, he said.
The countries that have moved up the value chain from sewing T-shirts to making computers became vulnerable to the whims of the markets in the industrialised world, he said.
South Korea, Singapore, and to a lesser extent, Taiwan, Thailand and Malaysia, were hard hit by the glut.
The adaptability of those economies to world market demand, however, will get them over this trough.

Recent political unrest in Indonesia and speculative attacks on the Thai baht have not triggered disinvestment or affected the ability of either country to finance their current account deficit, he said.
Current account deficits in the two countries result from the influx of huge foreign capital investments, whose reduction takes time as new export goods roll off the assembly line, Dalla said.
Asian countries also have large reserves to defend their currencies, he added.
LATIN TURNAROUND
The robust 7.2-percent growth in Mexican GDP in the second quarter pales in comparison to the slowest growth of the Asian tigers.

"Mexico's growth must be seen from the dismally low levels in 1995," said Shafiq Islam, emerging market strategist at Credit Suisse. Mexico's GDP slumped to 6.2 percent in 1995 in the wake of the peso crisis.
Quarter-to-quarter, Mexico's economy grew by about 1.0 percent, he said.
If the Mexican recovery stays on track, a 4.0-percent growth rate could be expected for this year, compared with the 6.0-percent for Singapore and 7.0-percent for Thailand, Islam said.

John Lonski, senior economist at Moody's Investors Service, said it was too early to tell if Latin American countries would emerge from last year's recession to embark on sustained growth. "Investors are wondering if the Latin countries have the political will to commit to structural reforms," said Lonski. "Or they still recoil in the face of change."
SHIFT IN PORTFOLIO INVESTMENTS
The Latin American turnaround story may be irresistible to portfolio managers whose performances are measured quarter to quarter, but evidence of portfolio reshuffling is spotty.

For the first half of 1996, the asset shift, based on a sample of 33 global emerging market funds by Peregrine Investments, came primarily from Asia to East Europe and Russia. The allocation to Asia declined from 43.7 percent to 40.6 percent, while East Europe rose from 16.6 percent to 19.0 percent. Latin America remained stable from 32.1 percent to 31.9 percent.
The outperformance in dollar terms of Latin equities over Asian equities could attract hot money to the Latin markets in the second half, the report indicates.

For fixed income investors, higher nominal yields of Latin American debts have always looked attractive relative to the staid papers from Asia, said Warren Allderige, managing director of Peregrine in New York.
But for credit quality and risk-adjusted portfolio investment, Asia still holds its place, he said.
Even for some nimble tactical asset allocation managers, Latin America as a whole stilll has not stood out.

"We raised our allocation to emerging markets in August because of global liquidity considerations," said Ken Ferguson at First Quadrant, Inc. "But there's no clear signal that Latin markets are more attractive."
According to the firm's proprietary model, India, Korea, Taiwan and Venezuela moved to the top, while Brazil, Chile, Mexico and the Philippines lingered at the bottom, he said.
HOPES FOR LATIN AMERICA
The economic recovery in Latin America this time around may stand a better chance of lasting than previous attempts, said David Rolley, a portfolio manager at Loomis Sayles in Boston.

"The peso crisis may have laid the foundation for a longer-term shift," he said. If the stop-and-go pension reforms finally succeed, investments from rising long-term domestic savings could enable Latin America to catch up.
Praveen of Merrill Lynch also ssees promising signs.
Inflation in Latin America is expected to remain stable and the region's current account deficit is likely to stick around two percent of GDP in 1996 and marginally higher in 1997, he forecast.
Declining country risk premiums, along with attractive opportunities afforded by privatisation, should draw strong foreign capital flow.
